# Interpretability in the Wild: From Fuzzy Logic to Alien Minds

Today's papers push interpretability beyond post-hoc heatmaps into the structural heart of models—differentiable fuzzy inference, symbolic geometry, and classification heads that read hidden states. A common thread is the tension between human-legible concepts and model-native representations, with several works arguing that interpretability must be engineered into architectures rather than retrofitted.

## Steering and Probing Model Internals

The question of whether generative inference is the right interface for classification tasks motivates **Reading Emotions in the Token Space** [2], which targets emotion recognition from speech in SpeechLLMs. Rather than decoding a label autoregressively, the authors attach a classification head to the final prompt token's hidden state, producing a label in one forward pass without modifying the backbone. Because the readout begins from the same hidden state the decoder would otherwise use, this yields a controlled comparison between generative and discriminative inference under otherwise identical conditions. The work matters because it shows that generative decoders can emit out-of-set labels and over-favor frequent classes—failure modes that a discriminative readout eliminates while preserving interpretability of the decision path.

A more radical reframing arrives in **Xeno-Interpretability** [3], which asks whether LLMs harbor internal structures for distinctions that have no adequate human concept. The authors distinguish the human-interpretable semantic space from a "xeno-semantic space" of model-native representations, formalizing these as xeno-representations. This is a conceptual provocation as much as a technical one: it implies that interpretability research anchored to human categories (truthfulness, refusal, deception) may systematically miss the model's actual computational vocabulary. The paper's contribution is to name and scope this blind spot, opening a research program around detecting and characterizing concepts that we cannot yet articulate.

## Fuzzy Systems and Differentiable Interpretability

**SoftTri** [4] addresses a long-standing friction in adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference systems: triangular membership functions offer interpretability, low parameter count, and strong locality, but their non-differentiability at knot points breaks gradient-based optimization. The authors introduce a smooth soft-hinge mechanism inspired by Swish-type activations to construct a differentiable triangular membership function, preserving the triangular shape's semantic clarity while enabling end-to-end learning. This matters for interpretability because it keeps fuzzy rules legible to humans without forcing practitioners to choose between transparency and trainability—an increasingly rare combination.

## Symbolic Structure for Explainable Perception

**NeuSOGA3D** [5] tackles 3D reconstruction from unorganized point clouds, where neural implicit methods achieve high accuracy but bury geometry in latent representations that resist interpretation and reuse in engineering workflows. The framework combines learned perceptual priors from NeuSOGA with explicit symbolic geometric reasoning, projecting point clouds onto principal structures to recover interpretable primitives. By hybridizing neural perception with symbolic abstraction, the method aims to produce reconstructions that are not only accurate but inspectable and editable within CAD-style pipelines. This matters because it demonstrates that neuro-symbolic integration can deliver explainability as a first-class output rather than an afterthought.

## Domain Knowledge and Structure-Aware Retrieval

**Enhanced Agriculture-informed Neural Network** [1] confronts N2O emission prediction, where complex interactions among soil, climate, biochemistry, and management practices resist both accurate modeling and physical interpretation. The proposed Knowledge-enhanced Agriculture-informed Neural Network injects domain knowledge into the architecture to improve generalization across environmental conditions while retaining physical interpretability—addressing the common critique that deep models capture nonlinearity at the cost of scientific legibility. For the interpretability community, this is a case study in constraining learned representations with structured priors, a strategy that trades some flexibility for robustness and trust.

**Q&A on Any Spreadsheet** [6] proposes splitting spreadsheets into interpretable chunks via semantic cell role annotation, improving chunking interpretability for LLM-driven RAG systems. Notably, the framework improves answer generation through enriched context rather than better retrieval, and it beats the state of the art—yet the author candidly identifies a hard ceiling. Because spreadsheets are two-dimensional unstructured data with continuous relationships and effectively infinite potential cell roles, any classifier restricted to finite pre-defined classes cannot fully capture the space. This negative result is itself a contribution: it delineates where classification-based interpretability breaks down and implicitly argues for open-ended, generative annotation schemes.

## Key Takeaways

- **Interpretability is increasingly architectural, not post-hoc.** SoftTri [4], NeuSOGA3D [5], and the agriculture-informed network [1] all build legibility into the model rather than extracting it afterward.
- **Generative decoders are the wrong tool for classification readouts.** The SpeechLLM emotion work [2] shows a discriminative head on hidden states fixes out-of-set labels and class-frequency bias with zero backbone modification.
- **Human concepts may be the wrong lens entirely.** Xeno-interpretability [3] argues for a model-native semantic space, challenging the assumption that interpretability means mapping to human categories.
- **Finite class taxonomies impose a hard ceiling.** The spreadsheet work [6] demonstrates that some domains—like 2D grids with unbounded cell roles—cannot be fully captured by pre-defined classification schemes.
- **Differentiability and interpretability can coexist.** SoftTri [4] resolves the long-standing trade-off between triangular membership functions' semantic clarity and gradient-based training.
- **Controlled comparisons are powerful methodological tools.** By isolating the readout mechanism while holding the backbone fixed, [2] cleanly attributes performance differences to inference style rather than model capacity.
- **Domain priors buy generalization and trust.** Injecting physical and geometric knowledge [1, 5] constrains representations in ways that improve cross-condition robustness while keeping outputs inspectable.

# Explainability in the LLM Era: When Reproducible Annotations Miss the Construct, When Agents Hide Their Reasoning, and When Transparency Becomes an Attack Surface

Today's explainability research is defined by a tension between measurement reliability and measurement validity: many methods produce stable, reproducible signals that nonetheless fail to capture the concepts they claim to explain. Across the papers below, we see this tension play out in institutional text analysis, chain-of-thought monitoring, sparse autoencoders for safety, and fairness auditing—alongside a growing countercurrent of attacks that weaponize transparency itself.

## Measuring What We Mean: Construct Validity, Subjective Tasks, and Human–Machine Gaps

Batzdorfer and Santagiustina address a foundational problem in LLM-based measurement: high annotation reproducibility does not imply that an LLM-inferred measure captures the intended construct [1]. Using European Commission AI Act consultation data that links structured survey responses to free-text submissions from the same stakeholders, they directly compare survey-reported measures against LLM annotations of the corresponding texts. Despite intraclass correlations above 0.99 for annotation reproducibility, the LLM-inferred measures show limited convergence with the survey-based constructs they were meant to approximate. This is a critical cautionary result for explainability research that treats stable LLM outputs as validated proxies for latent human attributes—reliability, they show, is not validity.

Guan and colleagues take on the complementary challenge of explaining models on inherently subjective tasks, where disagreement between annotators makes both evaluation and explanation ill-defined [2]. They propose a novel framework that combines differential testing—generating contrastive input pairs that isolate features driving model behavior—with annotation artifact construction to systematically map how models behave under annotator disagreement. The approach enriches interpretability by exposing where a model's decision boundaries align with or diverge from human disagreement structure, rather than treating disagreement as noise to be averaged away. Their work matters because subjective NLP applications (toxicity, sentiment, offensiveness) are precisely where one-size-fits-all explanations are most misleading, and where auditors most need to see the model's implicit stance.

Huang, Yu, and Ji argue that explainability should not be bolted on after the fact, but should be evaluated and optimized throughout the machine learning lifecycle, including at training time [3]. They provide a theoretical framework for explanation-driven learning, clarify the semantic interpretation of explanation quality at different training stages, and propose a practical method for transforming training data into a form that cultivates explainability in the resulting models. By tying explanation quality to the data and optimization pipeline rather than to post-hoc probes alone, the framework offers a design-level path toward models whose behavior is interpretable by construction.

## Chain-of-Thought as a Window—and a Veil—into Reasoning

Chen et al. investigate whether chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring, a cornerstone of current transparency practice, can be evaded for safety-critical risks such as biohazards [4]. They introduce a framework that simultaneously improves CoT monitorability and systematically tests evasion, decomposing CoT evasion into obfuscation (hiding suspicious reasoning) and diversion (misdirecting the monitor toward benign content). Testing across different model sizes and families, they find that evasion success varies substantially, highlighting that CoT faithfulness cannot be assumed. Their taxonomy-driven evaluation provides both a diagnostic instrument for monitor robustness and a warning that safety cases built on CoT oversight require adversarial validation.

Xu et al. push in the opposite direction, asking whether language models can learn to verbalize the hidden variables that drive their own behavior—and whether a "self-explanation" objective trades off against task performance [5]. They introduce a framework in which LMs are trained to explain their behavior in context by mapping internal representations to natural-language descriptions, hypothesizing that this strengthens both explainability and in-context reasoning. The work reframes explanation as a capability to be trained rather than a post-hoc artifact to be extracted, and probes the performance–interpretability trade-off directly. It connects the CoT monitoring literature to representation-level interpretability, suggesting that models can be incentivized to expose, not merely narrate, their internal states.

Bi, Li, and Wang contribute the Open Chain of Thought (OpenCoT) Benchmark, targeting a persistent weakness in explainability evaluation: existing CoT assessment tools are ad hoc, domain-specific, and hard to compare across tasks [6]. OpenCoT provides a standardized cross-domain evaluation framework designed to satisfy four criteria—reusability, comprehensiveness, comparability, and verifiability—with all tasks, annotation protocols, and evaluation scripts open-sourced. This kind of shared infrastructure is what allows claims about CoT quality (or CoT evasion, as in [4]) to be tested reproducibly rather than rhetorically.

## Interpretability Under Pressure: Sparse Features, Unknown Unknowns, and Controllability

Guo, Wang, and Chen confront a practical bottleneck in mechanistic interpretability: sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become the dominant tool for extracting monosemantic features from LLM activations, but they are expensive to train as model scale grows [7]. They introduce Sparse Attention Auto-Encoders (SAAEs), integrating sparse attention mechanisms into the SAE framework to overcome the expressiveness and efficiency limitations of existing designs. The work targets the scalability of feature extraction itself, which matters because interpretability pipelines that cannot keep pace with model scaling will inevitably lag behind the systems they are meant to illuminate.

Zhou et al. tackle "unknown unknown" failures in runtime verification—cases where a model's misbehavior stems from features and abstractions the designer never anticipated [8]. Their framework combines disentangled representation learning with an explanation-oriented reasoning mechanism to detect out-of-distribution inputs and provide understandable explanations for anomalous model behavior. By making the verifier itself explainable—not just the model—they extend interpretability into the monitoring stack, where explanations of *why an alert fired* are as important as explanations of predictions.

Akesson et al. address explainable AI planning (XAIP) from the opposite direction: instead of explaining a system's decisions to humans, they generate human-understandable versions of *human* behavior for a planner to consume [9]. Their approach formalizes plan explicability as a function of the explanation-generating planner's knowledge and assumptions, unified in a domain-independent planning framework, and evaluates it on two benchmarks. The careful reframing—explicability is relative to the explainer's model of the observer—provides conceptual tools that transfer well to human–AI explanation, where mismatched mental models are the central failure mode.

Wu et al. elevate interpretability from a diagnostic to a control signal, using explainability to identify the most relevant genes for drug response prediction, then feeding those genes back into model training [10]. This interpretability-guided optimization loop improves predictive performance while yielding biologically meaningful gene sets, demonstrating that explanations need not be a post-hoc cost center. The work is a strong existence proof that explanation and accuracy can be co-optimized rather than traded off, at least in domains where ground-truth relevance is partially knowable.

## Fairness Auditing, Personalization, and Explanation as Attack Surface

Panigrahi and colleagues examine explanation methods through a fairness lens, systematically evaluating whether explanation metrics (faithfulness, stability, etc.) behave equitably across demographic groups [11]. Their finding—that explanation quality is not uniformly distributed across groups—implies that interpreting a model through its explanations can itself produce inequitable conclusions, even when the underlying model appears fair by prediction-based metrics. This positions explanation equity as a distinct requirement for responsible XAI, one that current benchmarking practice largely ignores.

Anggara et al. bring explainability to personalized federated learning, where data heterogeneity across clients creates both privacy and interpretation challenges [12]. Their framework provides both intrinsic and post-hoc explanations tailored to personalized models, evaluated on real-world datasets. As personalized and federated deployment grows, per-client explanations become necessary for debugging and trust, and this work is one of the few to treat personalization and explainability as a joint design problem rather than separate concerns.

Doe et al. invert the usual framing of transparency as a good: they show that explainability mechanisms in text classification systems can be exploited as an attack surface, with explanations leaking information that adversaries use to craft more effective evasion attacks [13]. Their findings expose a genuine tension between the right to explanation and system security, suggesting that explanation outputs must be treated as a controlled channel with its own threat model. For regulators mandating explanation, this is an uncomfortable but essential result: transparency without access control can degrade the very robustness it is meant to support.

## Key Takeaways

- **Reproducibility ≠ validity.** LLM annotations can achieve near-perfect reproducibility (ICC > 0.99) while still failing to capture the intended construct, as shown on EU AI Act consultation data [1]. Explainability and measurement pipelines need construct-validity checks, not just reliability metrics.
- **CoT monitoring is not automatically faithful.** Evasion of chain-of-thought oversight via obfuscation and diversion is empirically feasible and varies by model, so safety cases built on CoT must be adversarially stress-tested [4]—ideally with standardized benchmarks like OpenCoT [6].
- **Explanations are relative to the explainer's model of the observer.** Framing explicability as a function of the explainer's knowledge and assumptions [9] clarifies why human–AI explanation failures are often mental-model mismatches rather than technical defects.
- **Interpretability can be a control signal, not just a diagnostic.** Using explanations to select features for retraining improves both accuracy and biological relevance in drug response prediction [10], challenging the assumed accuracy–interpretability trade-off.
- **Explanation quality itself has equity dimensions.** Faithfulness and stability of explanations vary across demographic groups [11], meaning XAI can propagate inequity even when prediction fairness metrics look acceptable.
- **Scaling interpretability is an engineering bottleneck.** Sparse attention autoencoders [7] and explanation-aware runtime verification [8] push back on the assumption that interpretability must lag behind model scale and deployment complexity.
- **Transparency is an attack surface.** Explanations can leak information that adversaries exploit for evasion [13], implying that explanation channels need their own threat models, access controls, and disclosure policies.

# Multimodal Research Digest: September 18, 2026

Today's multimodal landscape is defined by a decisive turn toward *structured heterogeneity*—researchers are no longer content to merely concatenate modalities, but are explicitly modeling the disagreements, asymmetries, and quality constraints between them. Alongside this, we see mounting pressure to make multimodal systems interpretable and trustworthy, from evidence-grounded assessments to posterior-aware evaluation of generative solvers. The recurring theme across all fifteen papers is that *what happens between modalities* matters more than what happens within them.

## Conflict, Discrepancy, and the Modeling of Cross-Modal Disagreement

Several papers this cycle treat inter-modal disagreement not as noise to be suppressed but as signal to be preserved and exploited.

The Modality Discrepancy Transformer (MDT) [1] targets ambivalence and hesitancy (A/H) recognition in clinical videos—affective states where facial, vocal, and linguistic channels genuinely contradict each other. Building on Bekhouche et al.'s conflict-aware fusion framework, MDT expands the token representation from 6 to 9 tokens, comprising three modality embeddings, three absolute-difference features, and three Hadamard-product interaction terms, so that cross-modal disagreement becomes an explicit input rather than an artifact destroyed by averaging. This matters because standard fusion methods systematically suppress exactly the contradictory signals that clinically trained observers use to detect ambivalence, and MDT demonstrates that architecture-level conflict encoding can recover them.

SAGG [16] approaches the same conceptual territory from a theoretical angle, studying heterogeneous corruption in multimodal learning. The authors prove that under a sample-heterogeneous corruption model—where different samples within a mini-batch have different modalities corrupted—any batch-level, sample-agnostic linear estimator with a shared modulation parameter incurs an irreducible bias relative to the clean-data gradient. They further show that sample-level all-or-nothing gating is the unique unbiased strategy within their framework, motivating a sample-adaptive gradient gating mechanism. This is a rare case where theoretical analysis directly pins down an architectural prescription for robust multimodal training.

TrioRAG [3] takes a different route to handling heterogeneous signals: rather than fusing them into a shared representation, it keeps three retrieval signals—the question, the anchor image, and a VLM-enhanced query synthesized from both—independent over a shared multi-vector index of page text and page images, combining results only through late fusion. The framework is graph-free, explicitly rejecting corpus-level graph construction as expensive, slow to query, and hard to maintain. The paper also contributes AutoQA, a multimodal automated question-answering evaluation component; together, TrioRAG suggests that for cross-document multimodal QA, disciplined late fusion of complementary retrieval views can outperform the heavyweight graph machinery that has dominated the space.

## Latent Spaces and Representation Learning Without Training

A cluster of work reimagines how multimodal representations are constructed and unified.

Uni-LaDiR [10] confronts a fundamental limitation of multimodal chain-of-thought: existing methods concatenate modality-specific thought tokens into a single sequence and hope the model bridges representational gaps on its own. Uni-LaDiR instead maps teacher reasoning steps from different modalities into a *shared latent thought space* via a unified encoder, with the encoder trained to preserve the information needed to later reconstruct or decode those thoughts. This reframes cross-modal reasoning as a latent-space alignment problem rather than a sequence-stitching problem, and is a promising direction for reasoning tasks where modality-specific token vocabularies are fundamentally incommensurable.

Lens [11] exploits a complementary insight: large autoregressive multimodal models, pretrained on massive corpora with instruction tuning, can already *select relevant evidence* and infer semantics under different task perspectives—so why train a dedicated embedding model at all? Lens proposes a training-free approach to multimodal representation learning that leverages these pretrained capabilities directly, addressing the data-scale gap between dedicated embedding models (trained on limited, less diverse data) and the massive corpora behind modern MLLMs. If it holds up, this could substantially reduce the cost of deploying high-quality multimodal retrieval in domains where labeled embedding training data is scarce.

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash [9] provides the infrastructure backdrop for these representational ambitions. It is a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts model with 552B backbone parameters, framed around the observation that long-horizon agent workloads are increasingly input-heavy and that prefill compute, KV cache HBM/SSD capacity, and data-transfer bandwidth now constitute the primary bottleneck to lowering deployment costs. The paper's focus on pushing KV cache compression to its limits makes it directly relevant to any multimodal system that needs to hold long visual-textual contexts in memory during multi-turn reasoning. The enormous author list reflects the scale of engineering effort that frontier multimodal serving now demands.

## Trust, Explainability, and the Evaluation Turn

Evaluation methodology is undergoing its own multimodal reckoning.

The unified trustworthiness framework of Raza et al. [4] argues that benchmark scores alone are an incomplete basis for assessing modern AI systems, and that LLMs, agentic systems, and MLLMs require *different* forms of assessment while still producing evidence that remains interpretable for development and oversight. The proposed framework connects output-level, trajectory-level, and cross-modal assessment through eight trustworthiness dimensions: capability, robustness, safety, fairness, transparency, governance, oversight, and efficiency. The key structural claim is that preserving system-level interpretability across these heterogeneous assessment types is not optional—it is what makes the evidence actionable for oversight bodies.

PosteriorBench [17] makes a parallel argument for generative inverse solvers in scientific domains. Current evaluations ask whether a method can produce a single plausible reconstruction, which is inadequate for ill-posed problems where many solutions are consistent with sparse or noisy observations; a method can achieve strong pointwise accuracy while failing to capture the true posterior through mode collapse, overconfident uncertainty, or averaging incompatible solutions. PosteriorBench shifts the evaluation target from point estimates to posterior matching, exposing failure modes that reconstruction-accuracy metrics structurally cannot see.

E-AVI [12] addresses the interpretability gap in automated video interview assessment, where numerical predictions alone offer little inspectable support for consequential hiring decisions. The framework extracts timestamped multimodal evidence and integrates dimension-conditioned evidence attention with source-level embeddings for scoring, with a shared evidence pool supporting natural-language feedback and follow-up question answering. On RecruitView and a private hospitality dataset, E-AVI consistently outperforms fine-tuned multimodal baselines in rank correlation—demonstrating that evidence-grounded architectures can improve accuracy and auditability simultaneously.

The hateful meme detection work of Xu et al. [5] identifies a concrete mechanism by which explainability *hurts* performance: existing explain-then-detect methods couple explanation generation and label prediction within the same training process, causing task-objective interference that degrades detection, sometimes below non-explainable baselines. Their progressive knowledge-to-decision alignment framework decouples these objectives, allowing the model to learn the implicit image-text interactions that carry hateful content before committing to a decision. This is a useful corrective to the assumption that explainable multimodal pipelines are merely less efficient versions of black-box ones.

## Multimodal Agents, Vehicles, and Embodied Environments

Three papers push multimodal systems into physical or persistent-world settings where consequences accumulate over time.

DeliveryGym [7] observes that for embodied agents, the consequences of an action extend beyond immediate task success—completing a delivery consumes time, energy, or money needed for later work. It introduces a 3D environment for evaluating and training agents on continuous courier shifts, coupling multimodal tool interaction with persistent world dynamics and computing trajectory-level feedback, supported by an adaptive curriculum. This matters because most embodied benchmarks reset the world between episodes, which structurally prevents agents from learning the resource-budgeting behavior that real deployment requires.

FedQoS [13] tackles multimodal in-cabin interaction in smart vehicles, where sensors range from high-bandwidth vision to low-rate physiological monitors and network QoS is heterogeneous and time-varying. Standard federated learning enforces rigid synchronous rounds that ignore these resource asymmetries, producing safety-critical timing violations and energy exhaustion. FedQoS introduces QoS-aware aggregation that respects these constraints—a necessary adaptation if collaborative multimodal training is ever to be practical in vehicular fleets.

The cognitive workload assessment framework of Gkikas et al. [14] offers a modality-agnostic hierarchical Transformer designed to process heterogeneous biosignal modalities within a single model, rather than building modality-specific pipelines. Their pilot study examines the effects of combining heterogeneous biosignals for workload measurement, an area they note remains under-explored despite extensive single-modality research. The modality-agnostic design is the notable contribution: it suggests a path to adaptive human-machine systems that can incorporate whatever biosignals happen to be available rather than requiring a fixed sensor suite.

## Memory, Personalization, and Applied Multimodal Systems

Long-horizon personalization and domain-specific retrieval round out the cycle.

ReaLMem [2] attacks the evaluation bottleneck in long-term multimodal personal memory, arguing that existing benchmarks are largely synthetic and text-only—overlooking the visual records that anchor everyday human memory—and lack the authentic, causally connected longitudinal data that real personalization demands, leaving them confined to shallow factual recall. The paper introduces a real-world multimodal personal archive benchmark intended to test not just remembering past events but tracking longitudinal experiences and evolving preferences. This distinction between *remembering* and *knowing* a user is a genuinely useful framing for companion AI research.

The medical case report system of Guo et al. [6] addresses a practical retrieval gap: millions of case reports in PubMed document rare diseases, diagnostic methods, and innovative treatments, but keyword-based tools struggle with unstructured, diverse case report text. Their system integrates structured clinical summaries with multimodal information, making case-report knowledge efficiently accessible. Given that case reports are often the only published evidence for rare conditions, improved retrieval here has direct clinical value rather than just benchmark relevance.

Finally, the offline RL work of Gao et al. [15] is included here for its relevance to multimodal embodied agents: it observes that standard regularization borrowed from computer vision fails to deliver in-distribution generalization and robustness for offline RL because low-level physical signals are highly sensitive to distributional shifts. Their boundary-aware data augmentation targets the overfitting-to-training-data problem directly. While not multimodal per se, the finding connects to the broader theme—techniques that work on high-level semantic representations do not automatically transfer to low-level continuous signals, and the mismatch is where robustness breaks down.

## Key Takeaways

- **Cross-modal disagreement is becoming a first-class modeling target.** MDT [1] and SAGG [16] both demonstrate that suppressing inter-modal conflict discards the most informative signal; SAGG goes further with a proof that batch-level, sample-agnostic gradient modulation is irreducibly biased under heterogeneous corruption, with all-or-nothing sample-level gating as the unique unbiased alternative.
- **Late fusion and training-free approaches are mounting a credible challenge to heavyweight graph and embedding pipelines.** TrioRAG [3] eliminates corpus-level graphs entirely, while Lens [11] argues pretrained MLLMs already encode enough representational capability to skip dedicated embedding training.
- **Evaluation is shifting from point predictions to distributions, trajectories, and evidence.** PosteriorBench [17], the unified trustworthiness framework [4], and E-AVI [12] all reject single-number assessment, targeting posterior matching, trajectory-level trustworthiness, and timestamped inspectable evidence respectively.
- **Explainability and accuracy need not trade off—but only if objectives are decoupled.** The hateful meme work [5] shows that coupled explain-then-detect training causes genuine interference, and that progressive knowledge-to-decision alignment recovers both.
- **Persistent-world agents require trajectory-level, not episode-level, feedback.** DeliveryGym [7] and FedQoS [13] both highlight that resource constraints accumulating across time—energy, time, bandwidth, QoS—are invisible to standard reset-per-episode or synchronous-round paradigms.
- **Long-term multimodal memory needs authentic longitudinal data.** ReaLMem [2] identifies synthetic, text-only benchmarks as the core bottleneck preventing progress from shallow factual recall toward genuine tracking of evolving user preferences.
- **Scale and efficiency remain coupled at the frontier.** DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash [9] frames KV cache compression, prefill cost, and memory bandwidth—not raw parameter count—as the binding constraints on multimodal agent deployment.
